# Introduction
Gradient boosting on decision trees is a form of machine learning that works by progressively training more complex models to maximize the accuracy of predictions. Gradient boosting is particularly useful for predictive models that analyze ordered (continuous) data and categorical data. Credit score prediction which contains numerical features (age and salary) and categorical features (occupation) is one such example.

Gradient boosting benefits from training on huge datasets. In addition, the technique is efficiently accelerated using GPUs. A large part of the production models at [Yandex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yandex) are trained on GPUs so we wanted to share more insights on our expertise in this area.

# Packages
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ISLR2)
library(bonsai)
library(catboost)
library(xgboost)
library(mbadtools)
# prefer `dplyr` for conflicts
conflicted::conflict_prefer_matching("select|filter", "dplyr", quiet=TRUE)
# advanced modeling
library(tidymodels)
# interpretation
source("gg_interpret.R")
```

# Data
```{r}
data(Boston, package="ISLR2")
Boston %>% skim_without_charts()
```

# Validation Setup
```{r}
set.seed(1353)
boston_split <- initial_split(Boston, prop = 3/4, strata = medv)
boston_train_data <- training(boston_split)
boston_test_data <- testing(boston_split)
```

# Model with `catboost`
```{r}
cat_spec <-
  boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.05) |>
  set_engine("catboost") |>
  set_mode("regression")
```

Boston model
```{r}
boston_fit <- fit(cat_spec, medv ~ ., data = boston_train_data)
boston_fit
```

```{r}
# make cat predictions
boston_pred = predict(boston_fit, new_data=boston_test_data)
# boston_pred %>% glimpse
# create an 'ugmented' prediction set
boston_aug = data.frame(boston_test_data, 
                        .estimate = boston_pred$.pred ) %>% 
  mutate(.resid = medv -.estimate, .std.resid = c(scale(.resid)))
# show first 10 
boston_aug %>% slice(1:10) %>% knitr::kable(digits=3)
```
# Model with `xgboost`

```{r}
xgb_spec <-
  boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.05) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |>
  set_mode("regression")

boston_xgb_fit <- fit(xgb_spec, medv ~ ., data = boston_train_data)
```

```{r}
# predictions
boston_xgb_pred = predict(boston_xgb_fit, new_data=boston_test_data)
# boston_xgb_pred %>% glimpse
# augment
boston_xgb_aug = data.frame(boston_test_data, 
                        .estimate = boston_xgb_pred$.pred ) %>% 
  mutate(.resid = medv -.estimate, .std.resid = c(scale(.resid)))
# show results
boston_xgb_aug %>% slice(1:10) %>% knitr::kable(digits=3)
```
# Model with `lm`
```{r}
lin_spec <-
  linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

boston_lin_fit <- fit(lin_spec, medv ~ ., data = boston_train_data)

# predictions
boston_lin_pred = predict(boston_lin_fit, new_data=boston_test_data)
# boston_lin_pred %>% glimpse
# augment
boston_lin_aug = data.frame(boston_test_data, 
                        .estimate = boston_lin_pred$.pred ) %>% 
  mutate(.resid = medv - .estimate, 
         .std.resid = c(scale(.resid)))
# display
boston_lin_aug %>% slice(1:10) %>% knitr::kable(digits=3)
```

# Metrics
```{r}
list(
  boston_aug %>% 
    metrics(truth = medv, estimate=.estimate) %>%
    gt() %>% tab_header(title="catboost") %>% wrap_table(),
  boston_xgb_aug %>% 
    metrics(truth = medv, estimate=.estimate) %>%
    gt() %>% tab_header(title="xgboost") %>% wrap_table(),
  boston_lin_aug %>% 
    metrics(truth = medv, estimate=.estimate) %>%
    gt() %>% tab_header(title="linear") %>% wrap_table()
) %>% wrap_plots()
```

`catboost` gives the best estimate, by all three metrics.

# YVP

```{r}
list(
  boston_aug %>% ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(medv, .estimate, color="cat"), shape=0, size=4)+
  geom_point(data=boston_xgb_aug,
             aes(medv, .estimate, color="xgb"), shape=1, size=4)+
  geom_point(dat=boston_lin_aug,
             aes(medv, .estimate, color="lin"), shape=2, size=4) +
  geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0, color="red", 
              linetype="dashed", linewidth=1.3) +
  labs(title="YVP for three Models",
       color="Model")+
  theme_bw()
) %>% wrap_plots()
```

# Conclusion

In a parsnip workflow `catboost` gives the best predictions.

# Feature Importance
Grab the average importances. For `catboost` we need to extract them from the fit object. For the others we can just use `vip::vi()`. The default is permutation importances.
```{r}
VI_cat = boston_fit$fit$feature_importances %>% as.data.frame()
VI_cat %<>% rownames_to_column(var="Variable")
VI_cat %<>% rename(Importance=V1)

VI_xgb = vip::vi(boston_xgb_fit)
VI_lin = vip::vi(boston_lin_fit)
```

Make the plots for comparison.
```{r}
list(
  VI_cat %>% gg_vip() + labs(title="catboost"),
  VI_xgb %>% gg_vip() + labs(title="xgboost"),
  VI_lin %>% gg_vip() + labs(title="linear")
) %>% wrap_plots(ncol=2) & theme(legend.position="none")
```

# Individual importance
The `lime` package is handy for this and makes nice graphs.
```{r warning=FALSE}
library(lime)
# pick an observation -- no 15
boston_obs = boston_test_data %>% slice(15)
boston_obs %>% knitr::kable(digits=3, caption = "Boston observation 15")

# Create an 'explainer' object using your training data and fitted model
explainer_cat <- lime(boston_train_data, boston_fit)
explainer_xgb <- lime(boston_train_data, boston_xgb_fit)
explainer_lin <- lime(boston_train_data, boston_lin_fit)
# Generate the explanation
explanation_cat <- lime::explain(boston_obs, explainer_cat, 
                                 n_features = 5)
explanation_xgb <- lime::explain(boston_obs, explainer_xgb, 
                                 n_features = 5)
explanation_lin <- lime::explain(boston_obs, explainer_lin, 
                                 n_features = 5)
```


```{r fig.height=8, fig.width=12, warning=FALSE}
# Plot the local explanation
list(plot_features(explanation_cat)+ labs(title="catboost"),
      plot_features(explanation_xgb)+ labs(title="xgboost"),
      plot_features(explanation_lin)+ labs(title="linear")
) %>% wrap_plots(ncol=2) & theme(legend.position="none")
```
